title: When Populism? Consistent and Opportunistic Populist Communication in the 2022 Brazilian Presidential Elections
abstract_excerpt: When do presidential candidates use populist communication, and does its prevalence vary across policy domains? We address these questions using an original dataset of 11,885 tweets from nine Brazilian presidential candidates during the 2022 elections. title: Skewed toward uniformity? Investigating algorithmic stereotyping and amplification in AI-generated images
abstract_excerpt: As text-to-image generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes visual communication, concerns are growing about its role in reproducing social stereotypes. While recent algorithm auditing studies have advanced our understanding of stereotypical AI-generated imagery, they have largely focused on a narrow set of stereotypes – primarily gender and race – overlooking more nuanced forms. title: From constituencies to audiences: lessons from Brazil about audience analytics in representative politics
abstract_excerpt: The pursuit of audiences is a key driver of the mediatization of politics, yet it remains unclear how parliamentarians carry out this task. Drawing on interviews with members of Brazil’s Congress, this study investigates how politicians incorporate audience analytics into their communication strategies. title: Branding the invisible: Big Tech, naming submarine cables, and the politics of infrastructure (in)visibility
abstract_excerpt: Submarine cables have historically been invisible: buried, technical and obscured by conventions such as security and language including naming practises that prioritised function over storytelling. However, as Big Tech companies like Google have emerged as major cable investors, increasingly shifting from consortium to sole or private ownership, they have disrupted the cable industry in many ways. abstract_excerpt: Political speeches are typically viewed as mobilizing democratic participation, yet research shows elite political rhetoric—particularly when it contains hate speech—may contribute to societal harm. Our study extends this line of research by investigating the association between hate speech and societal violence from a temporal perspective in the context of U.S. presidential campaigns. title: Gabriel Tarde’s Crowded Publics: Rediscovering the Work of a Forgotten Media Theorist
abstract_excerpt: Despite a revival of interest in the work of Gabriel Tarde, he remains an underappreciated, patchily translated, and often misrepresented thinker. When he is invoked, it is typically as the “forefather” of actor–network theory, as claimed by Bruno Latour; as the advocate of the power of conversation in media influence, as promoted by Elihu Katz; or as a useful, but inaccurate, citation for comparing rational publics with irrational crowds. abstract_excerpt: Online hate speech targeting minority groups poses a significant social identity threat to those affected, often prompting coping strategies like out-group avoidance or derogation, which can harm intergroup relations in diverse societies. abstract_excerpt: Recently, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have been positioning artificial intelligence as a utility that should be accessible to everyone. At the same time, they promote their cloud platforms as a means of ‘democratizing’ AI as they distribute easy-to-use AI services at scale. abstract_excerpt: Taking a configural approach to personal media use, this study examined how strong- and weak-tie media configuration relate to digital stress and well-being. title: Afterword: the waning power of the fix
abstract_excerpt: This commentary offers some reflections on the ‘power of the fix' in cybersecurity and its wider implications for technological democracy. title: Digital responsibility, skills and environmental awareness for digital sustainability
abstract_excerpt: This study investigates how digital competencies and environmental awareness interact to shape eco-friendly digital practices, contributing to the field of digital sustainability. title: Guidance over guidelines? Unpacking the uses and concerns of generative AI in communication science
abstract_excerpt: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) tools has transformed research practices across communication science. As genAI tools (and most notetably large language models), made the generation of text, images, and other media content extremely easy, they can potentially disrupt the way science is conducted. title: Predicting Irritation Disclosures in Romantic Relationships: Testing and Extending the Revelation Risk Model
abstract_excerpt: Feelings of irritation often emerge in romantic relationships. However, the theoretical mechanisms predicting whether individuals disclose these feelings to their romantic partner remain limited and largely reliant on examining indicators of future behavior rather than actual future behavior. title: Democratic Media Performance and Democratization: A Global Longitudinal Perspective
abstract_excerpt: Media that effectively perform their democratic functions are widely considered a key driver of democratization, yet longitudinal evidence on their impact remains limited. This study analyzed global annual time-series data on democratic media performance and democratization from 1946 to 2018. title: Political Actors and Their Media Practices: Analyzing the Role of Media Participation in Democratic Backsliding and Resilience
abstract_excerpt: This paper draws together insights from political science and political communication to advance a new understanding of the role of media in democratic backsliding and resilience. The central argument is that all political actors may also be media actors, although they may do so anonymously or use false identities. title: The “Netflix Look”: Moving image aesthetics as data under platform logic
abstract_excerpt: This article examines Netflix’s industrial model through the framework of platform logic, arguing that the data-centric approach it adopts in the production of moving images alters the creative process. The result is a conceptual shift from shooting a film to capturing an image. title: From platform outrage to institutional consequence: Convergent hybrid media accountability in Morocco
abstract_excerpt: This article develops the concept of convergent hybrid media accountability (CHMA) to explain how informal digital criticism is translated into institutional consequence in Morocco’s hybrid media environment. title: How social media produces “Cheap Europe”: Digital Balkanism and the politics of creator mobility
abstract_excerpt: Digital platforms increasingly mediate how socioeconomic unevenness becomes visible, often recoding structural inequality as consumable value. This article introduces the concept of digital Balkanism to explain how platformed travel content reworks long-standing intra-European hierarchies. title: When Past Hurt Meets Present Care: How Family History Shapes Adult Caregivers’ Communal Coping With Siblings in Their Caregiving for Parents With Health Challenges
abstract_excerpt: This sequential, explanatory mixed-methods study explores how adult caregivers’ perceived family functioning and unresolved hurt toward siblings from childhood are associated with their present-day communal coping (CC) with their siblings and caregiving outcomes. title: Does Office Type Determine Gendered Campaign Messages?
abstract_excerpt: This study examines how candidates’ gender shapes campaign messaging across different branches and levels of political office. Prior research offers mixed evidence on whether women are more likely than men to emphasize communal traits and women-related policies, often because gender effects are examined without fully accounting for institutional context. title: The Democratic Cost of Pursuing Virality: A Study into Parliamentary Communications
abstract_excerpt: The transformation of parliamentarians into media producers has heightened concerns about emerging forms of political communication. This mixed-methods paper examines the strategies they employ to enhance their digital presence. title: One-Dimensional Algorithm: Rereading Marcuse’s Critical Theory Through Platform Culture
abstract_excerpt: This article rereads Herbert Marcuse’s critical theory through algorithmic curation on commercial social media platforms, pursuing a dialectical argument in two directions: first, that platform capitalism structurally reproduces Marcuse’s diagnoses of false needs, incorporation, and one-dimensional thought; second, that platform dynamics exceed his framework—in its passive-subject assumptions, its vagueness about resistance, and its inability…

title: News Media, Narrative Authority, and the Global Ordering of Artificial Intelligence
abstract_excerpt: This article examines how mainstream Western news media structure global hierarchies of technological legitimacy in coverage of artificial intelligence (AI). Although AI circulates worldwide, its public meaning is shaped within a restricted geopolitical and linguistic sphere. title: “ In a way, I want TikTok to tell me what I want. . . ” Users’ experience of TikTok as a televisual algorithmic flow
abstract_excerpt: This article revisits Williams’s concept of flow, Firth’s notion of algorithmic flow, and Picone et al.’s concept of Small Acts of Engagement (SAOE) to examine how users experience TikTok’s algorithmic flow. SAOE are understood as low-effort, everyday acts through which users negotiate their identities and shape their digital consumption. abstract_excerpt: Abstract This study compares the effectiveness of narrative and non-narrative inoculation messages in reducing fatalistic beliefs and fostering resistance to conflicting cancer information. title: Are they virtue-signalling or sincere? The impact of perceived motives on the effectiveness of online collective action
abstract_excerpt: Social media is an important tool used by supporters of modern social movements to persuade others to participate. However, people who engage in online collective action often face speculation about their motives and may be perceived as acting for self-serving reasons. abstract_excerpt: This study examines how seven right-leaning media organizations utilize cross-platformization strategies to reach audiences across multiple platforms; in this case, Twitter and Truth Social.
